name: Poets, Painters and Rhythms of Latin America
description: From a Maya book of creation to Despacito: the writers, artists and musicians who made Latin America's culture heard around the world.

checkpoints.name: Old voices, new nations
checkpoints.note: The Popol Vuh, a Maya story of creation, is set down in writing in the sixteenth century, and Sor Juana writes her poems in colonial Mexico in the 1600s. Around 1880 the tango takes shape in the port cities of the Rio de la Plata, and the Cuban poet Jose Marti writes for independence in the 1890s.

checkpoints.name: Revolution and verse
checkpoints.note: The Mexican Revolution begins in 1910 and shapes the murals of Diego Rivera and the paintings of Frida Kahlo, who paints The Two Fridas in 1939. Borges in Buenos Aires, Neruda in Chile and Octavio Paz in Mexico write works that change Spanish-language literature, Carlos Gardel sings tango, and Celia Cruz grows up with Cuba's music.

checkpoints.name: Boom and bossa
checkpoints.note: The Cuban Revolution triumphs in 1959, and Celia Cruz leaves the island in 1960. In Brazil, bossa nova (1958), a gentle offshoot of samba, and The Girl from Ipanema (1962) become famous worldwide. Gabriel Garcia Marquez publishes One Hundred Years of Solitude in 1967, and with Vargas Llosa and magic realism Latin American fiction finds readers across the globe.

checkpoints.name: Old masters, new readers
checkpoints.note: Pablo Neruda wins the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971, Garcia Marquez in 1982 and Octavio Paz in 1990. Paulo Coelho's The Alchemist (1988) becomes a world bestseller, and in the 1990s the veteran Cuban musicians of the Buena Vista Social Club record an album that reaches listeners far beyond Havana.

checkpoints.name: Screens and streams
checkpoints.note: City of God (2002) shows life in the favelas of Rio, and Pan's Labyrinth (2006) mixes fairy tale with the Spanish Civil War era. Despacito (2017) becomes one of the most streamed songs in the world, showing how far Latin pop now travels.
